title: Keppard against Oliver: style and rival cliques
summary: They weigh Keppard against Oliver, noting Keppard's power and that Dreamland was a ballroom while Oliver played cabarets.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Yeah, in connection with Keppard there was always a lot of contention amongst the old timers as to whether Keppard kind of had a shade on the trumpet, or whether, no, Oliver was the right man and so forth. Mm-hmm. Did you have any feeling about that yourself? Or did they follow one after another, as Oliver and Louie really followed one after another?
Well, Joe was oldest, wasn't he?
I think Keppard was up here first. I don't know whether Keppard was older or not. I'm sure they were within a few years.

Uh-huh. Because, um… Well, it was too distinctly, distinctly style. The style was far apart. Keppard was a power man, Joe was playing. Yeah. But Keppard could play, but Keppard tell you I'll make the walls to him. Yeah, he was powerful.

He was powerful. And he had some of Joe's stuff too. Yeah, he had some things just like Joe. Because he, I don't know whether he liked Joe or whether they were jealous or not or not. But he had to admire Joe and he had some of Joe's stuff. As well as everybody else was. Well, you know how you fellows were in clicks.

Yeah. Everybody thought Ike was a top man. Yeah. Then somewhere else everybody thought McKendrick and so forth. Yeah. So there were clicks. Yeah. Like this. And I wondered if the same thing held for Oliver and Keppard. Maybe both of them were top men and what they could do.

Everybody liked them but well some guy right, maybe he worked with Joe or maybe he was in the night when Joe really cut up on the trumpet and he said well that's the greatest. Well see where we were in the harmonies and Greenman was a typical ballroom, it wasn't a cabaret. So we played more for dancing. In other words, there wasn't nothing but dancing there. And whereas Joe played in the cabaret, maybe he played more blues than we did, see, and more honky-tongue stuff. We played more popper tunes in the day but Freddie would jazz them up a little bit and then he'd take off on a few these high notes.
